lead_story.topic: Padres force NLDS Game 4 with dramatic 4-3 win — Brewers tying/go-ahead runs on base in 9th, Xander Bogaerts ends it with double play
lead_story.headline: Padres walk double-play tightrope to force Game 4

tweets.text: The Padres take Game 3 vs. the Brewers in the NLDS 👀

lead_story.research_notes: CONTINUING [Day 4]: San Diego staved off elimination in a thriller that had everything — lead changes, defensive wizardry, umpire controversy, and a walk-the-tightrope 9th inning where one swing could've ended the series. Jake Cronenworth put the Padres back in front with a HR (JomboyMedia calls it 'CRONE ZONE'). Manny Machado added insurance with an RBI (hit it 108.8 MPH, hardest ball of the game). Christian Yelich brought the Brewers back with a 2-out RBI single in the 7th — his FIRST playoff RBI since 2018 (TalkinBaseball). Michael King came in for the 8th inning of a must-win game after STARTING Game 2 two days ago. Threw 4 innings to close it out. The 9th inning had the drama: Padres walked two batters, putting the tying and go-ahead runs on base with Yelich at the plate. Xander Bogaerts turned a double play to end the game. Earlier controversy: Samad Taylor tapped his helmet (the ABS challenge signal) but the umpire didn't make him use it, and the Brewers were PISSED (JomboyMedia/TalkinBaseball). Jackson Merrill made multiple highlight-reel catches (TalkinBaseball: 'Pat Murphy has had enough of Jackson Merrill's defensive wizardry'). Mauricio Dubón robbed a ball that looked gone. Cooper Pratt committed a throwing error on a wonky play that scored an insurance run. Series now 2-1 Brewers, Game 4 Wednesday at Petco. One more chapter.
lead_story.gif_concept: Quiet resignation as the season teeters — the moment right before everything either clicks or collapses
lead_story.meme_concept: Padres facing bases-loaded, two-on in the 9th: sweating between two same-valence options (both terrifying). Choice not yet made — still sweating.

This is the end of the greatest international career in soccer history, and the grace note was perfect: one more goal, one more assist, one more reminder of what the world is losing.

supporting_stories.research_notes: Johnson announced his retirement after 14 seasons. Six-time Pro Bowl, five-time All-Pro (two first-team), two-time Super Bowl champion. Spent his entire career in Philadelphia. His statement: 'Right now, it is critical that I focus on my mental health. I owe it to my teammates, coaches, the organization and the fans to have my head and heart 100 percent in the game' (Schefter). Jeffrey Lurie released a statement (Schefter). ESPN: 'Another core piece of the Eagles' championship roster is now gone 💔.' AlbertBreer: Johnson arrived in junior college as a QB, got to Oklahoma as one, grew into a TE, then an OT, became an all-timer. BillBarnwell: He was comfortably the best player from the underwhelming top half of the 2013 first round. Research the 2013 draft top 10 — Eric Fisher, Luke Joeckel, Lane Johnson, Ziggy Ansah, Tavon Austin, Barkevious Mingo, Jonathan Cooper, Dion Jordan, Dee Milliner, Chance Warmack. Johnson is the only one who became a Hall of Fame-caliber player. Mental health disclosures from athletes are still rare enough to matter — this is significant. The Eagles are falling apart: lost the Super Bowl last year, now losing core pieces.
